teile.einleitung: Puberty is the time when a child becomes an adult. Hormones cause a growth spurt and the development of the sexual characteristics. Feelings, thoughts and the brain also change during this exciting time.
wichtigste: Typical of puberty are a growth spurt and the development of the sexual characteristics.
In girls it usually starts between 8 and 13 years, in boys a little later.
In boys the hormone testosterone is especially important.
In girls the ovaries produce mainly oestrogens.
The very first period is called menarche.
Boys’ voices break because the larynx and vocal cords grow.
Spots appear because the sebaceous glands produce more sebum.
Mood swings are normal in puberty.

abschnitte.text: **Puberty** usually starts in girls between 8 and 13 years and in boys between about 9 and 14 years. It lasts several years. Everyone has their own pace, and earlier or later are both normal. The word comes from the Latin pubertas, which means sexual maturity.

The brain gives the starting signal by stimulating the pituitary gland. This makes the sex glands produce more hormones. In boys the testicles produce mainly **testosterone**. In girls the ovaries produce mainly **oestrogens**.

There is a **growth spurt**, in which you can grow several centimetres a year. Hair grows under the arms and in the private area, and you sweat more. The sebaceous glands produce more sebum, so many teenagers get spots. Washing regularly helps, but spots often cannot be prevented completely.

In girls the breasts grow and the hips become wider. At some point the first period begins, the **menarche**. In boys the penis and testicles grow, the shoulders become broader and a beard begins to sprout. Because the larynx and vocal cords grow, boys’ voices **break** and become deeper.

The brain also changes a great deal in puberty. Feelings can become more intense, and moods sometimes swing quickly. Many teenagers want to become more independent and argue more often with their parents. This is a normal part of growing up, and it helps to talk about it with people you trust.

begriffe.erklaerung: A messenger substance that triggers changes in the body.
The very first period of a girl.
The time when boys’ voices become deeper.
A gland in the skin that produces an oily substance.
Physical features that distinguish women and men.

gewusst: Girls also get a slightly deeper voice in puberty, but you hardly hear it.
Teenagers often become tired later in the evening because their body clock shifts in puberty.
The part of the brain responsible for planning and reasoning is only finished at about 20 to 25 years.

teile.einleitung: Nodes of Ranvier are small gaps in the nerve fibres. They make sure that nerve signals are passed on especially fast. They are named after a French doctor.
wichtigste: A node of Ranvier is a gap between two sections of myelin.
It is only about 1 micrometre wide.
At the nodes there are especially many voltage-gated sodium channels.
The section between two nodes is called an internode.
In the peripheral nervous system, a node lies between two Schwann cells.
Nodes of Ranvier typically occur in vertebrates.

abschnitte.text: Nerve cells have long extensions, the **axons**. Many axons are surrounded by a fatty sheath, the **myelin**. It works rather like the insulation of a cable. But the sheath is not continuous: at regular intervals there are small **gaps**. These gaps are called **nodes of Ranvier**. They are only about **1 micrometre** wide, that is, one thousandth of a millimetre.

abschnitte.titel: The man who gave it its name
abschnitte.text: The nodes are named after the **French doctor** and researcher **Louis-Antoine Ranvier**. He described them in the 19th century when he examined nerve tissue under the microscope. Ranvier was very interested in the fine structure of tissues. His discovery later helped us to understand why some nerves are so fast.

The myelinated section between two nodes is called the **internode**. It is much longer than the node itself. In the **peripheral nervous system**, that is, in the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, one **Schwann cell** in each case forms the myelin of an internode. A node therefore lies between two Schwann cells. Right next to the node lies the **paranode**. There the loops of myelin are anchored to the axon.

At the nodes there are especially many **voltage-gated sodium channels**. Through them, sodium ions flow into the axon when a nerve signal passes. Under the myelin this hardly happens. That is why the signal jumps from node to node. This is called **saltatory conduction**, from the Latin word for jumping. In this way signals are passed on much faster and more economically than in nerve fibres without myelin.

Nodes of Ranvier typically occur in **vertebrates**, that is, in fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Many invertebrates have no such myelin sheath. Some of them, such as squid, achieve fast signals instead with especially thick nerve fibres. If the myelin in a human is damaged by a disease, for example in multiple sclerosis, the signals become slower.

gewusst: In the fastest nerve fibres of a human, signals travel more than a hundred metres per second.
Without myelin and nodes, our nerves would have to be much thicker to conduct equally fast.

teile.einleitung: Psychosomatics deals with the interaction of mind and body. Worries and stress can cause physical complaints, and physical illnesses can affect mood. The word is made up of the Greek words for soul and body.
wichtigste: Psychosomatics studies how mind and body influence each other.
The biopsychosocial model explains illness as an interplay of biological, psychological and social factors.
With lasting stress, the adrenal cortex releases more cortisol.
Tension headache is often partly caused by stress.
Positive expectations can have an effect: this is the placebo effect.
Negative expectations can strengthen complaints: this is the nocebo effect.

abschnitte.text: If you are excited, you may get a tummy ache. If you have had worries for a long time, you sleep badly or have a headache. **Psychosomatics** studies such connections. The word comes from the Greek “psyche” for soul and “soma” for body. Today illness is often explained with the **biopsychosocial model**: biological, psychological and social factors work together.

The researcher **Hans Selye** shaped the modern understanding of stress. He described the **“general adaptation syndrome”**: the body reacts to strain with alarm, adaptation and, if it lasts too long, exhaustion. With lasting stress, the **adrenal cortex** releases more of the hormone **cortisol**. In the short term it helps to provide energy. But if the stress lasts long, it can harm the body.

Some complaints are especially often partly caused by stress and tension. One example is **tension headache**, which feels like pressure around the head. The stomach and gut also often react sensitively. In a **somatoform disorder**, a person has physical complaints without doctors finding a sufficient physical cause. The complaints are real all the same and deserve good treatment.

It is astonishing how strongly expectations work. If someone firmly believes in a treatment, they may feel better even if the tablet contains no active ingredient. This is called the **placebo effect**. The other way round, negative expectations can cause or strengthen complaints. This is the **nocebo effect**. If you read a lot about side effects, for example, you sometimes notice them more.

In psychosomatics, body and mind are treated together. Besides medical treatment, talking, relaxation exercises and exercise often help. Enough sleep, breaks and time with friends protect against constant stress. In Switzerland, many hospitals have their own departments for psychosomatics.

gewusst: The word placebo is Latin and means “I shall please”.
Laughing and exercise can also help to break down stress hormones in the body again.

teile.einleitung: The pupil is the black hole in the middle of your eye. Light falls into the eye through it so that you can see. It can get bigger and smaller, depending on how bright it is.
wichtigste: The pupil lets light into the eye.
In bright light it gets smaller.
In the dark it gets bigger.
In humans the pupil is round.
It looks black because hardly any light comes back out of it.
Goats have horizontal pupils, cats in the daytime narrow slits.

abschnitte.text: Around the pupil lies the coloured **iris**. It is blue, green or brown, for example. The pupil itself is a hole in the iris. **Light** gets into the inside of the eye through this hole. At the back of the eye, the light hits the retina, which passes the images on to the brain.

The iris contains small muscles. They change the size of the pupil all by themselves. In **bright light** the pupil becomes **smaller**, so that not too much light falls into the eye. In the **dark** it becomes **bigger**, so that as much light as possible gets in. You can try this out: look into one eye in the mirror, close it briefly and open it again. The pupil first becomes large and then quickly smaller.

The pupil is not a black spot but an opening. It looks **black** because **hardly any light comes back out of it**. The light is almost completely swallowed up inside the eye. With photos taken with a **flash**, it is different: the bright flash hits the well-supplied layers of blood vessels at the back of the eye. Some of the red light comes back, and so **red eyes** appear in the photo.

In humans the pupil is **round**. In animals there are quite different shapes. **Goats** and sheep have **horizontal, elongated** pupils. This lets them survey their surroundings well and spot enemies early. The **domestic cat** often has a **narrow, slit-shaped** pupil in the daytime. In the dark it becomes almost circular and large.

gewusst: Eye doctors shine a small lamp into the eye to check whether the pupil narrows properly.
Cats’ eyes glow in the dark because behind their retina there is a layer that reflects light back.

teile.einleitung: Some people feel sick in a car, on a ship or on a plane. This is **travel sickness**. It is unpleasant but usually harmless and stops as soon as the journey is over.
wichtigste: The technical term for travel sickness is **kinetosis**.
Typical signs are nausea, paleness, sweating and dizziness.
It arises when the eyes and the sense of balance send conflicting messages to the brain.
In a car it helps to look out of the window into the distance.
On a ship it is best to sit in the middle.
Children of school age are especially often affected.
Ginger is often used as a natural remedy.

abschnitte.text: In technical language, travel sickness is called **kinetosis**, after the Greek word for movement. Depending on the means of transport, people also speak of seasickness or car sickness. Typical signs are **nausea**, yawning, cold sweat, a pale face and sometimes vomiting. The complaints often begin slowly and get stronger with time. After the journey they usually pass quickly.

In the inner ear sits the **balance organ**. It senses when the body moves or sways. But if you read a book in the car, your eyes report that you are standing still. The brain thus receives conflicting messages and reacts to them with nausea. That is why many people feel ill when reading or playing on their phone during a journey.

In a car it helps to look **out of the window into the distance**, because then the images from the eyes match the movement you feel. A seat at the front, fresh air and a light meal before the journey are also good. On a ship it is best to sit **in the middle**, because that is where it sways least. **Ginger** is often used as a natural remedy. For severe complaints there are also medicines from the chemist’s.

**Children of school age** suffer especially often from travel sickness. Small children under two, on the other hand, are rarely affected. In many people the tendency becomes weaker in adulthood. If you are exposed to a movement for longer, for example several days on a ship, you often get used to it.

Even in space there is a form of travel sickness. It is called **space sickness**. In weightlessness the balance organ lacks its familiar sense of up and down. Many astronauts therefore feel unwell in the first days. After that the body usually gets used to the new situation.

gewusst: The word “nausea” for sickness comes from the Greek word for ship.
In simulators and in games with VR goggles you can also get similar complaints.

teile.einleitung: Psychotherapy is the treatment of mental problems and illnesses using scientifically recognised methods, above all through conversation. There are different schools that differ in their ideas. What they all have in common is that a good relationship between therapist and patient is very important.
wichtigste: Sigmund Freud founded psychoanalysis.
The Swiss psychiatrist Carl Gustav Jung founded analytical psychology.
Carl Rogers developed client-centred talk therapy.
In systemic therapy, relationships in the social environment are at the centre.
The therapeutic relationship is seen as one of the most important factors that make therapy work.
Since 2022, basic insurance pays for psychological psychotherapy when a doctor refers the patient.

abschnitte.text: The Viennese doctor **Sigmund Freud** founded **psychoanalysis** around 1900. He assumed that unconscious wishes and conflicts influence our behaviour. In therapy they are meant to become conscious through conversation. An important term is **transference**: feelings from earlier relationships are directed at the therapist. These feelings can then be understood together.

The Swiss psychiatrist **Carl Gustav Jung** first worked together with Freud but then went his own way. He founded **analytical psychology**. Jung was especially interested in dreams, symbols and myths. Terms such as “introverted” and “extraverted” go back to him. He lived and worked for a long time in Küsnacht on Lake Zurich.

The American **Carl Rogers** developed **client-centred talk therapy**. He considered three basic attitudes to be central: **empathy**, that is, understanding with feeling, appreciation and genuineness. Another major school is **behavioural therapy**. It helps to change distressing thoughts and habits step by step. Today it is one of the best-studied methods.

**Systemic therapy** does not look only at a single person. At the centre are the **relationships in the social environment**, for example in the family, at school or at work. Problems are understood as part of a system. That is why several family members often take part in the sessions.

Research shows that one of the most important factors in every psychotherapy is the **therapeutic relationship**. You have to feel understood and safe. In Switzerland, the **referral model** has applied since July 2022. Since then, psychological psychotherapy has been paid for by **basic insurance** on **a doctor’s referral**. Before that, psychologists mostly had to work under medical supervision so that the health insurer would pay.

gewusst: Freud often had his patients lie on a couch so that they could relax and talk freely.
Today there are many different psychotherapy methods, which are studied scientifically.

teile.einleitung: Pro Juventute is a Swiss foundation that works for children and young people. Best known is its helpline 147. There, young people can always find someone who will listen.
wichtigste: Pro Juventute is a Swiss foundation for children and young people.
You can turn to the 147 helpline with any worries and questions.
The 147 helpline can be reached around the clock.
A call is free of charge, and the conversations are confidential.
You can also reach 147 by text message, chat and email.
Adults can find help from Dargebotene Hand (the Helping Hand) on the number 143.
In an acute emergency threatening life, you dial 144 for the ambulance service.

abschnitte.text: The name **Pro Juventute** comes from Latin and means “for the youth”. The organisation was founded in 1912 and is a **foundation**. It supports children, young people and their families all over Switzerland. This includes counselling, courses for parents and projects on subjects such as media, money or free time. Many people also know the **Pro Juventute stamps**, which the foundation sells to raise money.

The **147 helpline** is there for children and young people. You can get in touch with **any worries and questions**: arguments with friends, trouble at home, stress at school, heartache or simply a bad feeling. The helpline can be reached **around the clock**, also at night and at weekends. A call is **free of charge**. As well as by telephone, you can also get in touch by **text message, chat and email**.

The conversations with the 147 helpline are **confidential**. This means that what you tell them stays between those involved. You do not have to give your name. The specialists listen, take your worries seriously and look for solutions together with you. Sometimes it helps just to talk to someone about it. Nobody has to be left alone with their problems.

Besides 147, there are other numbers that you should know. **Dargebotene Hand** is there on **143** for adults who need someone to talk to. In an acute emergency threatening life, you dial **144** for the ambulance service. You reach the police on 117 and the fire brigade on 118. It is worth knowing these numbers by heart.

The history of Pro Juventute also includes a sad chapter. From 1926 to 1973 the charity project **“Kinder der Landstrasse”** (“Children of the Road”) took Yenish children away from their families. The Yenish are a minority in Switzerland who used to travel around a lot. Today this practice is seen as a serious injustice. The foundation has apologised for it.

gewusst: Every year the 147 helpline receives a very large number of enquiries from children and young people from all over Switzerland.
Pro Juventute has been issuing stamps for over a hundred years.

teile.einleitung: Prokaryotes are living things made of a single, very simply built cell. They have no cell nucleus. They include the bacteria and the archaea, the oldest forms of life on Earth.
wichtigste: Prokaryotes have no cell nucleus with a nuclear envelope.
They include the two domains of bacteria and archaea.
Their ring-shaped chromosome lies in the nucleoid.
They have smaller 70S ribosomes.
The cell wall of most bacteria consists mainly of murein.
Many move along using rotating flagella.

abschnitte.text: The word **prokaryote** comes from Greek and means roughly “before the nucleus”. In plants, animals, fungi and humans, the **eukaryotes**, the genetic material lies in a cell nucleus with a **nuclear envelope**. Prokaryotes have no such nucleus. Their cells are usually only a few thousandths of a millimetre across and so much smaller than most eukaryote cells. You can only see them under the microscope.

The prokaryotes make up two of the three great **domains** of life: the **bacteria** and the **archaea**. Bacteria live almost everywhere, in the soil, in water and in our gut. Many are useful, some make us ill. Archaea look similar to bacteria but differ in their metabolism and structure. Some live in extreme places, such as hot springs or very salty water.

The genetic material of a bacterium is usually a single **ring-shaped chromosome**. It lies freely in the cell plasma in an area called the **nucleoid**. In addition there are often small rings of DNA, the **plasmids**. They can carry features such as resistance to antibiotics. To make proteins, prokaryotes have **70S ribosomes**, which are smaller than the 80S ribosomes of eukaryotes.

Most bacteria have a firm **cell wall** made of **murein**. It gives the cell its shape and protection. Many bacteria move along using **flagella**. These are long threads that turn like a propeller. Bacteria usually multiply by simple cell division: one cell becomes two. Under good conditions this happens very quickly in some species.

The Danish doctor **Hans Christian Gram** developed a staining method in 1884 that is still important today. With the **Gram stain**, bacteria are divided into two groups according to the structure of their cell wall: Gram-positive and Gram-negative. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick layer of murein and stain dark violet. This helps doctors to choose the right antibiotic.

gewusst: On and in the human body there live roughly as many bacterial cells as there are body cells.
Prokaryotes existed on Earth for billions of years before there were plants and animals.

teile.einleitung: Primary urine is the first fluid that is filtered out of the blood in the kidneys. It is not yet urine: the body takes back almost all of it. Only a small remainder becomes the urine that we pass.
wichtigste: Primary urine is formed in the renal corpuscles when blood is filtered.
It resembles blood plasma, but without the large proteins.
About 99 per cent of the primary urine returns to the blood.
This process is called reabsorption.
Most of it is taken back in the proximal tubule.
In a healthy person, glucose is almost completely recovered.

abschnitte.text: Each kidney is made up of about a million tiny units, the **nephrons**. At the start of each nephron lies a tangle of fine blood vessels, the **glomerulus**. There, water with small dissolved substances is pressed out of the blood. Blood cells and large **proteins** stay in the blood because they are too big for the filter. The filtered fluid is the primary urine. In an adult about 180 litres of it are formed per day.

In its composition, primary urine is very similar to **blood plasma**, except that the large proteins are missing. It contains water, salts, glucose, amino acids and waste products such as urea. Because the dissolved particles are about as concentrated as in the blood, it is **isotonic** with blood plasma. If all of the primary urine were passed out, the body would very quickly lose far too much water and valuable substances.

That is why the body takes back about **99 per cent** of the primary urine. This process is called **reabsorption**. Most of it happens in the first section of the kidney tubules, the **proximal tubule**. Glucose is taken up there by **cotransport with sodium**: a transport protein carries sodium and glucose along together. Only about 1.5 litres of final urine are left each day, that is, the urine we pass.

In a healthy person, practically no glucose is found in the urine. But the transporters can only take up a certain amount. If the blood sugar rises above about **160 to 180 mg/dl**, they are overloaded and glucose appears in the urine. This limit is called the **renal threshold**. Sugar in the urine can be a sign of diabetes, which is why it is often tested for at medical check-ups.

gewusst: The kidneys filter a person’s entire blood supply many times a day.
From about 180 litres of primary urine, only around 1.5 litres of urine are produced each day.

teile.einleitung: Psychiatry is the field of medicine that deals with mental illnesses. These include, for example, depression, anxiety disorders or psychoses. Psychiatrists are doctors who recognise and treat such illnesses.
wichtigste: A psychiatrist is a doctor and may prescribe medicines, a psychologist may not.
The Burghölzli is the long-established university psychiatric clinic in Zurich.
The psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler coined the term “schizophrenia”.
Antipsychotics are mainly used against psychoses.
Lithium has long been used as a mood stabiliser in bipolar disorder.
A hallucination is a perception without an outside stimulus.

abschnitte.text: The two words sound similar but describe different professions. A **psychiatrist** has studied medicine and is a **doctor**. So she may **prescribe medicines**. A psychologist has studied psychology and treats mainly through conversation, if she has further training in psychotherapy. The two professions often work closely together.

In Zurich stands one of the best-known clinics in the world: the **Burghölzli**, today the University Psychiatric Clinic Zurich. It opened in 1870. The Swiss psychiatrist **Eugen Bleuler** worked there. At the beginning of the 20th century he coined the term **“schizophrenia”**. The young Carl Gustav Jung also worked at the Burghölzli.

In some mental illnesses, perception changes. A **hallucination** is a perception **without an outside stimulus**: someone hears voices, for example, although nobody is speaking. In a **psychosis**, a person temporarily loses touch with reality. In a **bipolar disorder**, phases of very low mood and very high mood alternate.

Mental illnesses are often treated with a combination of talking and medicines. Against psychoses, **antipsychotics** mainly help. In bipolar disorder, **lithium** has long been used as a mood stabiliser. Many people are treated as outpatients. A **day clinic** offers treatment during the day, and the patients spend the night at home.

Sometimes a person is in danger because of a serious illness but cannot see this for themselves. For such cases, Swiss law provides for **compulsory placement for care**. Here a person is taken to an institution for their own protection, even against their will. Strict rules apply for this, and the person concerned can have the decision reviewed by a court.

gewusst: Mental illnesses are common: many people are affected by them at some time in their lives.
The name Burghölzli goes back to a wooded hill in Zurich on which the clinic was built.

teile.einleitung: The forward roll is one of the first gymnastics exercises that children learn. You roll forwards over your rounded back. In PE lessons it is called a forward roll. In German it is also playfully called a Purzelbaum, a “tumbling tree”.
wichtigste: In PE the somersault-style roll forwards is called a forward roll (Rolle vorwärts).
Before rolling, you tuck your chin to your chest.
The back is round like a ball.
You place your hands shoulder-width apart in front of your feet.
You practise on a soft mat, and a sloping mat helps beginners.
If you roll backwards, the exercise is called a backward roll.

abschnitte.text: For a good forward roll, you crouch down. You place your **hands** on the floor **shoulder-width apart in front of your feet**. Then you tuck your **chin to your chest**, as if you wanted to look at your tummy. That way it is not your head but your neck that touches the mat first. Your **back** becomes **round like a ball** so that you can roll off gently.

In PE lessons the Purzelbaum is called a **Rolle vorwärts**, a forward roll. You push off gently with your legs and roll forwards over your rounded back. The knees stay close to the body. At the end you come down on your feet and stand up, if possible without using your hands. In the **backward roll**, you roll the other way, backwards over your back.

Forward rolls are practised on a **soft mat**, never on a hard floor. For **beginners** a **sloping mat** is especially helpful: because it goes slightly downhill, you almost roll by yourself. At the beginning the teacher can help by supporting your back and neck. It is important never to put your whole weight on your head.

abschnitte.titel: From the roll to the somersault
abschnitte.text: The forward roll is a basis for many other exercises in floor gymnastics. Anyone who can do the roll safely later learns rolls with a run-up or a roll over an obstacle. A **somersault** is a flip **in the air** in which the hands do not touch the floor. That is much harder and needs a lot of practice and help from experts.

gewusst: The word Purzelbaum has been known for several centuries.
The forward roll trains balance and body awareness, which also helps in many other sports.

teile.einleitung: Before a cell divides, it has to double all of its genetic material. This process is called **replication**. Many enzymes work together in it, like in a small factory.
wichtigste: In replication, the DNA of a cell is doubled.
Replication is **semi-conservative**: each new double helix keeps one old strand.
Meselson and Stahl proved this in 1958 using heavy nitrogen.
Helicase unwinds the DNA at the replication fork.
DNA polymerase always extends a strand from 5' to 3'.
DNA ligase joins the Okazaki fragments together.

abschnitte.text: DNA is a **double helix** of two strands that looks like a twisted ladder. In replication the two strands separate, and a matching new strand is built for each. Each new double helix therefore consists of one old and one new strand. This kind is called **semi-conservative**, that is, half preserving. The researchers **Matthew Meselson** and **Franklin Stahl** proved this in 1958 with bacteria and heavy nitrogen.

The place where the DNA opens is called the **replication fork**. There the enzyme **helicase** unwinds the double helix and separates the two strands. In front of the fork, the DNA would become more and more twisted as a result, like a twisted telephone cable. **Topoisomerase** prevents this by releasing the tension. Other proteins hold the separated strands apart.

The new strand is built by **DNA polymerase**. But it cannot simply start from nothing. First the **primase** makes a short RNA starting piece, the primer. The polymerase then attaches building block after building block, always in the direction **from 5' to 3'**. These numbers name the two ends of a DNA strand.

Because the polymerase works in only one direction, it can build one of the two strands in one go. The other it builds in short pieces called **Okazaki fragments**. They are named after the Japanese researchers, the Okazakis. **DNA ligase** then joins these pieces into a continuous strand. In the end, two complete DNA molecules have been formed.

Many DNA polymerases have a **proofreading function**. They check every new building block and remove wrongly built-in ones again at once. As a result the error rate in replication is very low. If a mistake still remains, it is called a **mutation**. Other repair systems of the cell later correct many such mistakes.

gewusst: With every division, a human cell has to copy about three billion base pairs.
So that this goes fast enough, replication begins at many places on the DNA at the same time.

teile.einleitung: In an accident or emergency, every minute counts. The **chain of rescue** describes what has to happen one after another so that a person gets the best help. Every link is important, and the first links are in the hands of all of us.
wichtigste: The classic chain of rescue begins with immediate life-saving measures.
After the emergency call comes first aid.
For helpers, their own safety has top priority.
With the Rautek grip you pull an unconscious person out of danger.
The chain of survival of the European Resuscitation Council has 4 links.
In many cantons, first responders are alerted by smartphone app.

abschnitte.text: The classic chain of rescue begins with the **immediate life-saving measures**, such as securing the scene of the accident. Then comes the **emergency call**, in Switzerland the number **144** for the ambulance service. After that comes **first aid** until experts arrive. The **rescue service** follows, and finally treatment in **hospital**. If one link fails, the whole chain is weakened.

For all helpers, their **own safety** has top priority. If you are injured yourself, you can no longer help anyone. On Swiss motorways, you put up the **warning triangle** at least **100 metres** behind the scene of the accident. A high-visibility vest makes helpers easier to see. Only when the place is secured do you look after the injured.

Sometimes an unconscious person has to be quickly taken out of a danger zone, for example out of a car. For this there is the **Rautek grip**. You reach through from behind under the armpits and take hold of one forearm of the person. In this way you can support them with your own body and pull them away. With an unconscious motorcyclist wearing a **full-face helmet**, you carefully take off the helmet so that they can breathe freely.

For cardiac arrest there is a chain of its own, the **chain of survival**. At the European Resuscitation Council it consists of **4 links**: recognition and emergency call, early chest compressions, early defibrillation and treatment afterwards. In **telephone resuscitation**, the emergency call centre guides laypeople over the telephone through the chest compressions. So nobody has to decide alone what to do.

In many cantons there are **first responders**. These are trained volunteers who are alerted by **smartphone app** when someone nearby has a cardiac arrest. They begin resuscitation **before the rescue service arrives**. Often they are on the scene faster than the ambulance. In this way the person affected gains valuable minutes.

gewusst: In cardiac arrest, the chance of survival falls markedly with every minute without help.
The Rautek grip is named after the Austrian jiu-jitsu teacher Franz Rautek.

teile.einleitung: A right-handed person is someone who prefers to do most things with the right hand. This applies to the great majority of people. That is why many objects and habits in everyday life are designed for right-handers.
wichtigste: Most people are right-handed.
A right-hander writes with the right hand.
The right hand is controlled mainly by the left half of the brain.
In right-handers the right hand is usually a little stronger.
Even small children often prefer to grasp and draw with one hand.
In Switzerland you usually shake hands with the right hand as a greeting.

abschnitte.text: Our brain has two halves. Interestingly, the **left half of the brain** mainly controls the **right** side of the body, and the right half the left. In right-handers the left half is especially well practised for fine hand movements. That is why writing, drawing or throwing with the right hand works better for them. This hand is usually also a little **stronger**.

Whether a child will be right-handed can often be seen early on. The child mostly **grasps and draws with the right hand**. But the preferred hand is often only quite certain at nursery or school age. A right-hander **writes with the right hand** and also uses it for most other activities. The great majority of people are right-handed, and only about one in ten is left-handed.

Many things in everyday life are designed for right-handers. When you lay the table, the **knife is on the right** of the plate and the fork on the left. The **computer mouse** is usually **to the right** of the keyboard. Scissors, tin openers and fountain pens are also often built for the right hand. In Switzerland you usually shake **hands** with the **right hand** as a greeting.

abschnitte.titel: Right and left are equally good
abschnitte.text: In the past, left-handed children were often forced to write with the right hand. Today we know that this **retraining** can do harm. That is why children are allowed to write with the hand that comes naturally to them. For left-handers there are special scissors and writing tools. A few people can use both hands almost equally well.

gewusst: In many animals too there are preferences for one side, for example in the paws of cats or dogs.
Experts call the preferred hand handedness.

teile.einleitung: Proprioception is the perception of the position and movement of your own body. Thanks to it, you know where your arms and legs are even with your eyes closed. In German it is also called Tiefensensibilität (deep sensitivity).
wichtigste: Proprioception means perceiving the position and movement of your own body.
In German it is also called Tiefensensibilität.
It includes the sense of position, the sense of movement and the sense of force.
Muscle spindles report how far a muscle is stretched.
Golgi tendon organs in the tendons measure how hard a muscle is pulling.
Exercises on a wobbly surface train proprioception.

abschnitte.text: Besides sight, hearing, smell, taste and touch, we have other senses. One of them is **proprioception**. It constantly tells the brain how the joints are positioned and how the body is moving. Because the sense organs lie deep in muscles, tendons and joints, it is also called **deep sensitivity**. We hardly notice this sense because it always works in the background.

Proprioception is counted as three partial senses. The **sense of position** tells you how your joints are positioned at the moment, for example whether your arm is bent. The **sense of movement** reports whether and how fast a part of the body is moving. The **sense of force** helps you to judge how much force you need, for example to lift a glass or a heavy bag.

The information comes from special sense organs. **Muscle spindles** lie in the muscle and report how far it is stretched. **Golgi tendon organs** sit in the tendons and measure how hard the muscle is pulling. There are also sensors in the joint capsules. The brain combines all these reports with what the eyes and the sense of balance supply.

A doctor can test proprioception easily: you close your eyes and bring your **index finger to your nose**. If this works well, the sense is working properly. If a leg has “gone to sleep”, the feedback about its position is missing, which is why you stumble easily. After a **ligament injury to the foot**, people often train with exercises on a **wobbly surface**, such as a cushion or a balance board. That way the foot learns again to adjust safely.

gewusst: The term proprioception comes from the Latin “proprius”, which means “own”.
Without proprioception you would have to keep looking at your own feet when walking.

teile.einleitung: The prefrontal cortex is the front part of the cerebral cortex, right behind the forehead. It helps us to plan, make decisions and control impulses. It is one of the areas of the brain that take the longest to mature.
wichtigste: The prefrontal cortex lies in the frontal lobe, behind the forehead.
It is important for planning, deciding and controlling impulses.
Working memory depends heavily on it.
According to what we know today, it matures until about the mid-twenties.
The messenger substance dopamine is especially important for it.
The case of Phineas Gage showed in 1848 how important this area is for personality.

abschnitte.text: The cerebrum is divided into lobes. At the very front lies the **frontal lobe**, and its foremost part is the **prefrontal cortex**. The word cortex means bark or rind. One part of it lies directly above the eye sockets and is called the **orbitofrontal cortex**. It helps to judge whether something is worth it, for example a reward.

The prefrontal cortex is often described as a control centre. It helps with **planning**, **deciding** and **impulse control**. If you sit down to do your homework even though you would rather play games, it is working especially hard. **Working memory** also depends heavily on it. It lets you keep information ready for a short time, such as a telephone number while you type it in.

The brain does not develop all at once. The prefrontal cortex is one of the areas that take the longest. According to what we know today, it is fully mature only at **about the mid-twenties**. This partly explains why teenagers sometimes act more spontaneously and judge risks differently from adults. Over time, the connections in this area get better and better.

Nerve cells pass on signals using messenger substances. For the prefrontal cortex, **dopamine** is especially important. It influences attention and motivation. In **ADHD**, medicines such as **methylphenidate** are used, which strengthen the effect of dopamine. They can help people to concentrate better.

In 1848 the American railway worker **Phineas Gage** had an accident: an iron rod went through the front of his brain. He survived, but his personality changed greatly. The case showed how important this part of the brain is. Later the Portuguese doctor **Egas Moniz** developed the **prefrontal leucotomy**, an operation on the frontal brain, and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1949. The operation often had serious consequences and is seen today as a wrong path.

gewusst: The skull of Phineas Gage and the iron rod are still kept today in a museum of Harvard University.
In humans the frontal lobe is larger in proportion to the brain than in most other animals.

teile.einleitung: After training, the body needs time to recover. This recovery phase is called **regeneration**. It is only during this time that the body really becomes stronger and more capable.
wichtigste: Regeneration is the recovery of the body after strain.
In active regeneration you move gently, for example by easy cycling.
Sauna, massage and sleep count as passive regeneration.
Gentle cooling down helps to break down lactate faster.
Carbohydrates refill the glycogen stores in the muscles.
Muscle soreness is usually strongest one to three days after training.

abschnitte.text: There are two kinds of recovery. In **active regeneration** you move gently, for example by easy cycling, walking or calm swimming. The strain is so low that the body does not tire. In **passive regeneration** the body rests, for example when sleeping, in the sauna or during a massage. The two forms complement each other well.

With very intense strain, more **lactate** is formed in the muscles, a substance from the breakdown of sugar without enough oxygen. Many athletes jog gently for a few more minutes after a race. The light movement keeps the blood flow high, and so lactate is broken down faster than in complete rest. Even after the strain has ended, you go on breathing faster for a while. This increased oxygen uptake is called **EPOC**.

When you sweat, the body loses water and **electrolytes**, above all sodium, which is a component of table salt. After a lot of sweating, a drink with a little salt therefore helps. In the muscles, energy is stored as **glycogen**, a storage form of glucose. After training, **carbohydrates** such as bread, rice or pasta refill these stores. A little protein also supports the repair of the muscles.

**Muscle soreness** is caused by tiny injuries in the muscle fibres. It occurs especially easily with braking, so-called **eccentric** work, in which the muscle gets longer under tension, for example when running downhill. The pain comes with a delay and is usually strongest 24 to 72 hours after the strain. In English it is therefore called DOMS, which means delayed onset muscle soreness. After a few days it disappears by itself.

Some athletes step into an ice bath after training. This **cold water immersion** makes the blood vessels narrower and can dull pain. Whether it helps the body in the long term is disputed among experts. Undisputedly important, on the other hand, is enough **sleep**. In sleep the whole body recovers especially well.

gewusst: A muscle does not become stronger during training but in the recovery time afterwards.
If you train too much and recover too little, you can even become weaker in time.

teile.einleitung: **Retroviruses** are special viruses that build their genetic material into the genetic material of the infected cell. To do so they take an unusual route: they rewrite RNA into DNA. The best-known retrovirus is HIV.
wichtigste: Retroviruses carry single-stranded RNA in the virus particle.
The enzyme reverse transcriptase rewrites this RNA into DNA.
Integrase builds the virus DNA into the genetic material of the host cell.
The built-in virus DNA is called a **provirus**.
HIV is the best-known retrovirus that makes humans ill.
About 8 per cent of human genetic material consists of remains of old retroviruses.

abschnitte.text: In cells, genetic information is normally copied from **DNA** into **RNA**. Retroviruses do it the other way round, hence the name: “retro” is Latin and means backwards. Their genetic material consists of **single-stranded RNA**. In the host cell, the enzyme **reverse transcriptase** rewrites this RNA into DNA. An enzyme is a protein that carries out chemical processes.

The newly formed virus DNA travels into the cell nucleus. There the enzyme **integrase** builds it into the genetic material of the host cell. The built-in virus DNA is called a **provirus**. The cell now reads it like its own genes and makes new viruses. Because the provirus is firmly lodged in the genetic material, it is very hard to get rid of a retrovirus completely.

The best-known retrovirus that makes humans ill is **HIV**, the human immunodeficiency virus. It infects mainly the **T helper cells**, important cells of the immune system. Over time more and more of these cells are lost, and the defences become weaker. Without treatment this can lead to the disease **AIDS**. Today there are medicines that suppress the virus strongly, and many of them inhibit precisely the reverse transcriptase.

Reverse transcriptase was discovered in **1970**. Two researchers found it independently of each other: **Howard Temin** and **David Baltimore**. Before that people thought that genetic information always flows only from DNA to RNA. For their discovery the two received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1975, together with Renato Dulbecco. Today reverse transcriptase is also an important tool in research laboratories.

In the course of evolution, retroviruses have left traces in the genetic material again and again. Such remains are called **endogenous retroviruses**. About **8 per cent** of human genetic material consists of them. Most of them have long been broken and can no longer make viruses. Some of these old virus genes even do useful jobs in the body today.

gewusst: The human genetic material contains more remains of old viruses than genes that carry the instructions for proteins.
Retroviruses also exist in animals such as cats, chickens and mice.

teile.einleitung: The quadriceps is the large muscle at the front of the thigh. It is one of the strongest muscles in the body. Without it we could neither stand up nor climb stairs or jump.
wichtigste: The quadriceps lies at the front of the thigh.
It has four heads, hence its name.
Its main job is to straighten the knee.
The kneecap is embedded in its tendon.
The rectus femoris also spans the hip joint.
Its opposing muscle is the muscle group at the back of the thigh.

abschnitte.text: The name **quadriceps** comes from Latin and means “four-headed”. The muscle really does consist of **four heads**, that is, four partial muscles. They lie **at the front of the thigh** and join at the bottom into one shared, strong tendon. This tendon runs over the knee and attaches to the shinbone. The quadriceps is one of the largest muscles of the human body.

The **main job** of the quadriceps is to **straighten the knee**. You need this when standing up, walking, running and jumping. It works especially hard when **climbing stairs**, cycling and in a knee bend. One of its heads, the **rectus femoris**, also spans the **hip joint**. That is why it also helps to lift the leg forwards at the hip.

A special bone is embedded in the tendon of the quadriceps: the **kneecap**. It acts like a pulley. This allows the muscle to pull on the knee with more leverage. The kneecap also protects the knee joint from the front. Below the kneecap, the tendon continues to the shinbone.

Muscles often work in pairs. The opposing muscle of the quadriceps is the **muscle group at the back of the thigh**, which bends the knee. Doctors test the quadriceps with a well-known test: a light tap with a small hammer on the tendon **below the kneecap** triggers a reflex. The **lower leg shoots forwards**. This shows whether nerves and muscle work well together.

gewusst: The quadriceps is the muscle that is often especially strongly developed in footballers and cyclists.
The kneecap is the largest sesamoid bone of the human body, which is what bones lying inside a tendon are called.

teile.einleitung: The **emergency blanket** is a thin, shiny foil that belongs in every first aid kit. It is folded up tiny but can cover an injured person completely. In this way it protects them from the cold.
wichtigste: An emergency blanket is usually gold on one side and silver on the other.
It consists of a very thin plastic foil.
It protects injured people above all from the cold.
You find it in the first aid kit, also in the car.
Because it is light and small, it belongs in the rucksack on mountain hikes.
Rescuers can see the shiny blanket from far away.

abschnitte.text: An emergency blanket is usually **gold** on one side and **silver** on the other. It consists of a **very thin plastic foil** coated with a wafer-thin layer of metal, mostly aluminium. The foil is thinner than a sheet of paper. Folded up, it fits into a trouser pocket. Spread out, though, it is about as big as a duvet.

An injured person cools down quickly, especially if they lie still. The emergency blanket **protects against the cold**. It reflects body heat back and keeps out wind and rain. You **cover the injured person with it** and wrap it as closely as possible around the body. It is also important that the injured person does not lie directly on the cold ground.

The emergency blanket is in every **first aid kit**, for example in the car first aid kit, at school or in the sports club. Because it is **light and small**, it also belongs in the rucksack on every **mountain hike**. In the mountains the weather can change quickly. If you are injured and have to wait for help, you will be glad of the protection.

The shiny foil helps in another way too. It reflects light and so is **visible from far away**. This makes it easier for rescuers to find an injured person, for example from a helicopter. In Switzerland, after an accident in the mountains, you call Rega on the number **1414**. In any emergency, though, the first rule is: stay calm and get help.

gewusst: The foil of the emergency blanket was originally developed for space travel.
An emergency blanket weighs only about as much as a letter, around 50 grams.

teile.einleitung: Rega is the Swiss Air Rescue. With its red and white helicopters it helps people in need, especially in the mountains. In Switzerland you can alert it on the number 1414.
wichtigste: Rega stands for the Swiss Air Rescue service (Rettungsflugwacht).
You alert Rega on the telephone number 1414.
Rega was founded in 1952.
It mostly comes by helicopter, especially often in the mountains.
Its helicopters are red and white.
On a mission a doctor goes along.
Supporters back Rega with an annual contribution.

abschnitte.text: **Rega**, the **Swiss Air Rescue**, rescues people from the air. Mostly it comes by **helicopter**. This matters above all where an ambulance cannot get to, or only slowly. It helps especially often **in the mountains**, for example after accidents while hiking, climbing or skiing. But it also flies patients quickly to a hospital, for example after serious road accidents.

In Switzerland you alert Rega on the number **1414**. On the telephone you say who you are, where you are and what has happened. The operations centre then decides what help is needed. On a mission a **doctor** goes along, together with a pilot and a paramedic. This means that treatment can begin at the scene of the accident. It is worth knowing the number 1414 by heart.

Rega’s helicopters are **red and white**, like the Swiss flag. This means you can recognise them from far away. Rega has bases spread across the whole of Switzerland so that a helicopter can be anywhere as quickly as possible. For flights at night the crews use **night vision goggles**. With these they can see obstacles such as cables or rocks even in the dark. With its own aircraft, the ambulance jets, Rega also brings sick or injured people back from abroad.

Rega was founded in **1952**. Since then it has rescued many thousands of people. At the beginning it also flew with small aeroplanes and dropped rescuers by parachute. Soon the helicopter became the most important means of rescue in the mountains. Today Rega is a **charitable foundation**.

To a large extent Rega is supported by **patrons**. These are people who pay it an **annual contribution** every year. Millions of people in Switzerland take part, often whole families. Thanks to this support, Rega can be ready around the clock. Under certain conditions, patrons have the costs of a mission waived.

gewusst: Rega is ready for action around the clock on every day of the year.
More than a third of the people in Switzerland support Rega as patrons.

teile.einleitung: The cartwheel is a popular gymnastics exercise in which you turn sideways over your hands. Arms and legs move like the spokes of a wheel. With a little practice, many children manage it in the garden or on the meadow.
wichtigste: In a cartwheel, hand, hand, foot, foot touch the ground one after the other.
You move sideways.
In the air the legs are straight and spread apart.
For a short moment the arms carry the whole weight.
The exercise is called a wheel because arms and legs turn like spokes.
A line on the ground helps to do the cartwheel straight.

abschnitte.titel: Why it is called a wheel
abschnitte.text: In German the gymnastics exercise is called **Rad**, a wheel, because **arms and legs turn like spokes** around the middle of the body. Seen from the side, you see a star that turns round once. You also say “turning a cartwheel”. You move **sideways**, not forwards. The cartwheel is an important basic exercise in floor gymnastics.

You take a run-up and hold your **arms high above your head**. Then you place the first hand on the ground, and straight after it the second. The legs swing one after the other over the body. For a short moment **the arms carry the whole weight**. After that one foot lands first, then the other. The order is therefore **hand, hand, foot, foot**. In the air the legs are **straight and spread apart**.

At the beginning the cartwheel is often still crooked. A **line on the ground** helps a lot: hands and feet should all land on this line. It can be a piece of tape in the gym or a line drawn in chalk. Strong arms and good body tension are also important. It is best to practise on a mat or on soft grass.

If you can do the cartwheel well, you can make it harder. For example, you can do it **with one hand only**. An important further development is the **round-off**: here you make a quarter turn and land on **both feet at the same time**. In artistic gymnastics the round-off is often done before somersaults to build up momentum.

gewusst: Practised gymnasts can even do the cartwheel completely without hands, which is called an aerial cartwheel.
Many children first learn the cartwheel on the meadow before they practise it in the gym.

teile.einleitung: An **ambulance** brings help to sick and injured people and drives them to hospital. In Switzerland it is also called the **Sanität**. With blue lights and siren it gets quickly through the traffic.
wichtigste: In Switzerland an ambulance is often called an **Ambulanz**.
The emergency number for the ambulance service in Switzerland is **144**.
Trained paramedics work in the ambulance.
The vehicle is equipped like a small mobile treatment room.
When blue lights and siren are on, other vehicles must make way.

abschnitte.text: In Germany people mostly say Rettungswagen. In Switzerland it is often called **Ambulanz** or simply **Sanität**. The emergency number for the ambulance service is **144** all over Switzerland. In the emergency call centre, experts decide which vehicle sets off. In serious emergencies, an emergency doctor sometimes goes along as well.

Inside the vehicle there is a **stretcher** on which the patient lies. There are also devices for measuring pulse and blood pressure, oxygen and a **defibrillator**, which can get a stopped heart going again. Bandages and medicines are also on board. The **paramedics** are specially trained for this. They can already help a great deal on the way.

In an emergency, the ambulance drives with **blue lights** and **siren**. Then all other vehicles must make way and form a lane. If you are on foot, you wait at the side of the road. Cyclists are also best off stopping. This way the help reaches its destination quickly.

gewusst: The word “ambulance” comes from the Latin “ambulare”, which means to walk about.
For accidents in the mountains or far from the nearest hospital, Switzerland also has rescue helicopters.

teile.einleitung: Some people recover especially well after hard times. This inner strength is called **resilience**. The good news: you can practise and strengthen it.
wichtigste: Resilience is the ability to cope well with crises.
The word comes from the Latin “resilire”, to spring back.
Emmy Werner researched resilience in a long-term study on the island of Kauai.
A stable person to rely on strengthens children’s resilience especially.
Resilience is not inborn and unchangeable, it can be strengthened throughout life.
Resilience is often compared to a tumbler toy that always springs upright again.

abschnitte.text: In psychology, **resilience** means the ability to cope well with crises and difficult experiences. The word comes from the Latin **“resilire”**, which means to spring back or bounce off. Resilient people also experience grief and stress. But after a while they find their balance again. In a picture, it is compared to a **tumbler toy**, which stands up again after every knock.

The subject became well known through the psychologist **Emmy Werner**. She followed children on the Hawaiian island of **Kauai** who were born in 1955 over decades. Many of them grew up under difficult conditions. Some of these children nevertheless developed well and became contented adults. Werner studied what had helped these children.

Such helpful circumstances are called **protective factors**. Especially important is a **stable person to rely on**, that is, someone who is reliably there. This can be a parent, but also grandparents, a teacher or a coach. Other protective factors are good friendships and the feeling of being able to do something. Someone who can ask for help is also better equipped.

Resilience includes a particular way of looking at problems. Resilient people mostly see problems as **solvable**. They concentrate on what they themselves can influence. They take feelings seriously but do not let themselves be steered entirely by them. And they believe that difficult times pass again.

Resilience is **not inborn and unchangeable**. You can strengthen it throughout life. A simple exercise is to write down **three good things** from the day every evening. This directs your attention to what has gone well. Enough sleep, exercise and good conversations with people you trust also help.

gewusst: In engineering, resilience describes how well a material returns to its old shape after being deformed.
The Kauai study followed about 700 children for about 40 years.

teile.einleitung: The body has to regulate its blood pressure and amount of water well. A chain of hormones and enzymes helps with this: the **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system**, or **RAAS** for short. Many blood pressure medicines act at exactly this point.
wichtigste: The enzyme renin is made in the kidney.
Renin is released mainly when the blood pressure in the kidney falls.
Renin splits the protein angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.
The angiotensin-converting enzyme, ACE for short, turns this into angiotensin II.
Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex makes the kidney take back more sodium.
ACE inhibitors and sartans are important blood pressure medicines.

abschnitte.text: The kidney constantly measures how much blood arrives at it. If the blood pressure in the kidney falls, it releases the enzyme **renin**. An **enzyme** is a protein that speeds up chemical processes. In the blood, renin splits the protein **angiotensinogen**, which comes from the liver. This produces **angiotensin I**.

Angiotensin I itself has hardly any effect. The **angiotensin-converting enzyme**, or **ACE** for short, changes it into **angiotensin II**. Angiotensin II narrows the blood vessels, and the blood pressure rises. It also stimulates the adrenal gland to make another hormone. In this way several substances work together like the links of a chain.

**Aldosterone** is made in the **adrenal cortex**. In the kidney tubules it makes sure that **more sodium** is taken back into the blood. With the salt, more water also stays in the body. This increases the amount of blood and so the blood pressure. In this way the whole system helps to make up for blood pressure that is too low.

With high blood pressure, the RAAS can be slowed with medicines. **ACE inhibitors** block the enzyme ACE so that less angiotensin II is formed. A typical side effect is a dry **irritating cough**. The **sartans**, on the other hand, block the angiotensin II receptor, the docking point of the hormone. Both groups are among the most common blood pressure medicines.

gewusst: The first ACE inhibitor, captopril, was developed on the model of a substance from the venom of a South American pit viper.
Renin was discovered as early as 1898, long before the whole system was understood.

teile.einleitung: Rickets is a disease in which children’s bones stay soft and become deformed. The most common cause is a lack of vitamin D. Today rickets is rare in Switzerland, because it can be prevented well.
wichtigste: The most common cause of rickets is vitamin D deficiency.
The body makes vitamin D itself when sunlight falls on the skin.
Vitamin D helps to absorb calcium from the gut.
Typical signs are bowed legs and thickenings on the ribs.
In Switzerland, babies are given vitamin D drops daily to prevent it.
In adults the softening of the bones is called osteomalacia.

abschnitte.text: For strong bones, the body needs **calcium**. So that it can absorb calcium from the gut, it needs **vitamin D**. The special thing is that the body makes most of its vitamin D itself when **sunlight falls on the skin**. Only a few foods, such as oily fish, contain a lot of it. If vitamin D is missing, the bones do not become properly hard. In children this disease is called **rickets**.

Because the bones are soft, they can bend under the body’s weight. Children with marked rickets often have **bowed legs**. On the ribs there are knobbly thickenings called the **rachitic rosary**, because they look like the beads of a rosary. The children often grow more slowly and are weaker. In adults a similar softening of the bones is called **osteomalacia**.

In the **19th century** rickets was very common in the industrial cities of Europe. **Smoke** from factories and **narrow alleys** kept out the sunlight. Many children also worked in dark rooms. As a remedy they were given **cod liver oil**, an oil from the liver of fish that contains a lot of vitamin D. Many children, however, found its taste horrible.

Today we know exactly how to prevent rickets. In Switzerland it is recommended to give **babies** in their first year of life **vitamin D drops every day**. Later, exercise outdoors and a balanced diet help. Because of this prevention, rickets has become rare here. In some countries of the world, however, it is still widespread.

gewusst: Vitamin D is really more of a hormone, because the body can make it itself.
In winter the sun in Switzerland is often too weak for the skin to make enough vitamin D.

teile.einleitung: A reflex is a fast, automatic reaction of the body to a stimulus. You do not have to think about it, the body reacts by itself. The path that the signal takes is called the reflex arc.
wichtigste: At the start of every reflex arc is a sensory receptor that picks up a stimulus.
Many reflexes are fast because they are switched over in the spinal cord.
Motor nerve cells pass the signal from the spinal cord to the muscle.
In the knee-jerk reflex the lower leg shoots forwards.
In the knee-jerk reflex only one synapse in the spinal cord is passed through.
The blink reflex protects the eye.

abschnitte.text: A **reflex arc** has several stations. At the start is a **sensory receptor** that picks up a stimulus, for example pressure or stretching. A sensory nerve cell passes the message to the **spinal cord**. There the signal is switched over. **Motor nerve cells** then pass the command to the **muscle**, which contracts. The brain often only learns afterwards what has happened.

Many reflexes happen very fast because they are **switched over in the spinal cord**. The signal does not first have to take the long route to the brain and back. This is important for protection: if you touch a hot hob, you pull your hand back in a flash. Only a moment later do you feel the pain consciously.

The best-known reflex is the **knee-jerk reflex**. The doctor strikes the tendon below the kneecap with a small hammer. This briefly stretches the thigh muscle, and the **lower leg shoots forwards**. In this, only **one synapse** in the spinal cord is passed through, that is, one connecting point between nerve cells. Because stimulus and reaction take place in the **same muscle**, it is called a **monosynaptic stretch reflex**.

Many reflexes protect us. The **blink reflex** closes the eyes when something suddenly approaches fast. Coughing and sneezing are also reflexes: they carry dust and foreign bodies out of the airways. The swallowing reflex makes sure that food goes into the gullet and not into the windpipe.

Besides inborn reflexes there are also learned ones. The Russian researcher **Ivan Pavlov** studied them using **dogs**. He noticed that dogs produce saliva as soon as they expect food. If a signal always sounded before feeding, the dogs soon produced saliva at the signal alone. Pavlov called this a **conditioned reflex**. He received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1904, but for his research on digestion.

gewusst: With the small hammer, doctors check whether nerves and spinal cord work properly.
The knee-jerk reflex is also called the patellar reflex, after the Latin word for kneecap.

teile.einleitung: In the brain there is a small control centre, the **hypothalamus**. It sends messenger substances to the pituitary gland and in this way gives it orders. These messenger substances are called **releasing hormones**.
wichtigste: Releasing hormones are made in the hypothalamus.
They make the pituitary gland release its own hormones.
TRH makes the pituitary release TSH, and CRH makes it release ACTH.
GHRH promotes the release of growth hormone, and somatostatin inhibits it.
Most releasing hormones are peptides, that is, short chains of protein.
TRH consists of only 3 amino acids.

abschnitte.text: The **hypothalamus** is a small part of the diencephalon. Directly beneath it hangs the **pituitary gland**. The hypothalamus makes hormones that reach the pituitary through fine blood vessels. These **releasing hormones** order it to release certain hormones of its own into the blood. The hormones of the pituitary then control other glands in the body in turn.

**TRH** (thyrotropin-releasing hormone) makes the pituitary release **TSH**. TSH stimulates the thyroid gland. **CRH** is also called **corticoliberin** and leads to the release of **ACTH**. ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex to produce the stress hormone cortisol. **GHRH** promotes the release of **growth hormone**.

The hypothalamus can not only drive but also brake. Such substances are called inhibiting hormones. **Somatostatin** inhibits the release of growth hormone. The messenger substance **dopamine** inhibits the release of **prolactin** from the pituitary. In this way the body keeps the amounts of hormones in balance.

Most releasing hormones belong to the **peptides**. These are short chains of **amino acids**, the building blocks of proteins. TRH is especially small and consists of only **three amino acids**. Other releasing hormones are much longer. Because they work in very small amounts, researching them was difficult.

gewusst: For discovering hormones of the hypothalamus, Roger Guillemin and Andrew Schally received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1977.
Releasing hormones work even in tiny amounts, far less than a millionth of a gram.

teile.einleitung: After digestion, the food building blocks are small enough to get into the blood. This uptake through the gut wall is called **absorption**. It takes place mainly in the small intestine.
wichtigste: Most nutrients are absorbed in the small intestine.
Tiny bulges, the microvilli, form the brush border and enlarge the surface.
Glucose gets into the gut cell together with sodium.
For vitamin B12, the intrinsic factor from the stomach is needed.
Fats and the vitamins A, D, E and K first go into the lymphatic system.
The portal vein brings sugar and amino acids first to the liver.

abschnitte.text: The **small intestine** is the most important place of absorption. Its inner wall is strongly folded and covered with finger-shaped **villi**. The gut cells themselves carry even tinier bulges, the **microvilli**. Together they form the **brush border**. This creates a very large surface through which nutrients are taken up.

**Glucose**, that is, grape sugar, gets into the gut cell by **secondary active transport**. That means it is carried through a transporter together with **sodium**. **Fructose**, fruit sugar, takes a different route via the transporter **GLUT5**. Proteins are broken down into amino acids and small pieces. Di- and tripeptides, that is, chains of two or three amino acids, get into the cell together with protons via **PepT1**.

Fats do not dissolve in water. With the help of bile, they form tiny droplets, the **micelles**. The fat-soluble **vitamins A, D, E and K** also need these micelles to be absorbed. In the gut cell, the fats are packed into transport packages, the **chylomicrons**. These first get into the **lymphatic system** and only later into the blood.

Sugar and amino acids go straight into the blood. The **portal vein** collects this blood from the gut and brings it first to the **liver**. The liver checks the substances, stores some of them and makes harmful substances harmless. Only after that does the blood reach the rest of the body. In this way the liver is a kind of checkpoint.

**Vitamin B12** needs a helper to be absorbed. The parietal cells of the stomach make the **intrinsic factor** for this. Vitamin B12 binds to it and is only absorbed in the last section of the small intestine. If the intrinsic factor is missing, a deficiency of B12 can arise. Such a deficiency can lead to anaemia.

gewusst: The inner surface of the small intestine is about as large as a small flat, around 30 to 40 square metres.
A large part of the water is only taken back from the food pulp in the large intestine.

teile.einleitung: Prions are special disease-causing agents. They are neither bacteria nor viruses, but consist only of protein. They can cause serious diseases of the brain, in animals and in humans.
wichtigste: Prions consist of misfolded protein.
They multiply by making normal proteins fold incorrectly as well.
Stanley Prusiner coined the term prion and received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1997.
BSE in cattle also concerned Switzerland in the 1990s.
In humans, prions cause for example Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
Prions survive many common sterilisation methods.

abschnitte.titel: A protein in the wrong shape
abschnitte.text: Proteins are long chains that fold into a particular shape. Only in the right shape can they do their job. A **prion** is a protein that is folded wrongly. The special thing is this: when it meets a normal protein of the same kind, it makes that protein fold wrongly too. This creates a chain reaction. The misfolded proteins clump together and little by little damage the **brain**.

For a long time people believed that every disease-causing agent needs genetic material. The American researcher **Stanley Prusiner** put forward the idea that a protein alone can be infectious. He coined the word **prion**, a short form of the English for proteinaceous infectious particle. At first his idea was very controversial. In 1997 he received the **Nobel Prize in Medicine** for it.

The best-known prion disease in animals is **BSE**, popularly called mad cow disease. In the 1990s there were cases of BSE in Great Britain and also in **Switzerland**. The authorities took strict measures, for example they banned feeding meat-and-bone meal to cattle. In sheep and goats there has been a prion disease called **scrapie** for a very long time.

In humans, **Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease** is the best-known prion disease. It is very rare but takes a severe course. One form of it was linked to BSE. In **Papua New Guinea**, a disease called **kuru** appeared among one people. It was passed on through certain mourning rituals and disappeared when these customs were given up.

Prions are surprisingly resistant. They survive many common **sterilisation methods** that are otherwise used to kill bacteria and viruses. That is why surgical instruments must be treated in a special way, or even thrown away, if prions are suspected. In hospitals strict rules apply for this.

gewusst: Prions have no genetic material of their own and can still spread in the body.
For his research on kuru, the American Carleton Gajdusek received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1976.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland every person must have health insurance for basic cover. For many households the premiums are a heavy burden. With the individual premium reduction, the Confederation and the cantons help people with lower incomes.
wichtigste: IPV stands for individual premium reduction.
The premium reduction is paid for by the Confederation and the cantons.
The cantons decide who is entitled to it and how much they get.
Premiums for children from households with low and middle incomes are reduced by at least 80 per cent.
For young adults in training it is at least 50 per cent.
The Confederation pays 7.5 per cent of the gross costs of basic insurance towards the premium reduction.
In 2024 the voters rejected the Premium Relief Initiative.

abschnitte.text: Since 1996 the Health Insurance Act, or **KVG** for short, has applied in Switzerland. Since then **basic insurance** has been compulsory for everyone. The premium does not depend on income: a person with a small wage pays the same as a person with a large wage with the same insurer and the same plan. So that premiums stay affordable for households with little money, there is the **individual premium reduction**, or **IPV** for short.

The premium reduction is paid for jointly by the **Confederation and the cantons**. The Confederation pays a fixed contribution of **7.5 per cent** of the gross costs of basic insurance. The cantons add money of their own. Because every canton has its own rules, the support can be very different depending on where you live.

The **cantons** decide who is entitled to a premium reduction and how high it is. Mostly they look at taxable income and assets. In some cantons the reduction is paid out automatically, in others you have to make an application. The money usually goes straight to the health insurer, which then sends a lower bill.

For families there are rules set by the Confederation. For households with low and middle incomes, the cantons must reduce the premiums of **children** by at least **80 per cent**. For **young adults in training** it is at least **50 per cent**. This is meant to make sure that families with children are not burdened too heavily.

How much premiums should be reduced is a matter of political dispute. In 2024 Switzerland voted on the **Premium Relief Initiative**. It wanted to make sure that nobody has to pay more than **10 per cent** of their disposable income on premiums. Supporters saw it as necessary relief, while opponents warned of high costs for the Confederation and the cantons. The voters rejected the initiative.

gewusst: A considerable share of the people in Switzerland receive a premium reduction.
The health insurance premium in Switzerland is a per-head premium: it is paid per person, not according to income.

teile.einleitung: Red blood cells live for only a few months and have to be replaced constantly. Very young red blood cells are called **reticulocytes**. Their number in the blood shows how busy the bone marrow is.
wichtigste: A reticulocyte is a young red blood cell without a nucleus.
It still contains ribosomal RNA, which the mature erythrocyte lacks.
Classically, reticulocytes are made visible with brilliant cresyl blue.
In a healthy person, about 0.5 to 2 per cent of the red blood cells are reticulocytes.
After about 1 to 2 days in the blood, a reticulocyte becomes a mature erythrocyte.
In aplastic anaemia the reticulocyte count is greatly reduced.

abschnitte.text: In technical language, red blood cells are called **erythrocytes**. They arise in the **bone marrow** from precursors. One of these precursors is the **normoblast**. It expels its cell nucleus and thereby becomes a **reticulocyte**. This then gets into the blood.

The reticulocyte no longer has a nucleus but still contains **ribosomal RNA**. With the dye **brilliant cresyl blue**, this remaining substance becomes visible as a fine network. That is where the name comes from: “reticulum” is Latin and means little net. The reticulocyte circulates in the blood for about **1 to 2 days**. Then it loses the RNA and is a mature erythrocyte.

In a healthy person, about **0.5 to 2 per cent** of the red blood cells are reticulocytes. Doctors measure this value in a blood test. It shows how many new red blood cells are just being made. In this way you can tell whether the bone marrow is working well. Today measuring machines usually count the cells automatically.

After **blood loss**, the reticulocyte count rises markedly. This shows that the bone marrow is increasing blood production to make up for the loss. If the count is greatly reduced, on the other hand, the bone marrow is making too little blood. One example is **aplastic anaemia**, a rare disease in which the bone marrow hardly makes any blood cells any more. Anaemia is a shortage of red blood cells.

gewusst: Every second, the body of an adult makes about two million new red blood cells.
A mature red blood cell lives for about 120 days.

teile.einleitung: Pyjamas are the clothes that you put on to sleep in. They are comfortable and keep us pleasantly warm at night. In Germany people often say Schlafanzug (sleep suit).
wichtigste: Pyjamas are clothes for sleeping in.
They usually consist of a top and trousers.
Pyjamas originate in India.
Cotton is popular because it is soft and absorbs sweat.
In Germany people often say Schlafanzug.
A long shirt for sleeping in without trousers is called a nightshirt.

abschnitte.text: **Pyjamas** usually consist of two parts: a **top** and **trousers**. They come with long sleeves and legs for the winter or short for warm summer nights. You put them on because they are **comfortable and clean**. The clothes from the day stay outside, and you sleep more pleasantly.

Pyjamas originate in **India**. The word comes from Persian and means roughly “leg garment”. At first it meant wide, light trousers. British travellers brought these clothes to Europe in the 19th century. There they gradually became the sleepwear that we know today.

**Cotton** is very popular for pyjamas. It is **soft**, pleasant on the skin and **absorbs sweat**. In winter there are also pyjamas made of thicker, fluffy fabric. **Warm socks** help against **cold feet**. What matters is that you can move freely in them and neither freeze nor sweat.
