In Switzerland people mostly say **Pyjama**, in Germany often **Schlafanzug**. If you prefer to wear a long shirt without trousers, you sleep in a **nightshirt**. In the past many people wore such nightshirts, often with a nightcap. Today there are pyjamas in all colours and with patterns, from stars to animals.

gewusst: The word pyjamas is spelt differently in different countries, in American English for example “pajamas”.
Some children and adults have pyjama parties, at which everyone stays the night together in their pyjamas.

teile.einleitung: A reflex is an automatic, unconscious reaction of the body to a stimulus. One example is pulling your hand away in a flash from something hot, which is controlled through the spinal cord. Reflexes protect us before we can even think.
wichtigste: A reflex is an automatic, unconscious reaction to a stimulus.
Many reflexes run through the spinal cord and not through the brain.
That is why they are especially fast.
The path of a reflex is called a reflex arc.
The knee-jerk reflex is often tested by the doctor with a small hammer.
Babies have special reflexes that disappear later.
Reflexes protect the body from injuries.

abschnitte.text: A **reflex** is a reaction that always happens in the same way and without thinking. If you touch a hot hob, you pull your hand away before you properly feel the pain. If something flies towards your eye, the eyelid closes by itself. Such reactions can hardly be suppressed by will.

The path of a reflex is called the **reflex arc**. A sensor in the skin reports the stimulus along a nerve to the **spinal cord**. There the signal is switched directly to a nerve that leads to the muscle. The brain only finds out afterwards, which is why the reflex is so fast.

In the **knee-jerk reflex**, the doctor taps with a small hammer just below the kneecap. The lower leg then shoots forwards. In this way she can check whether nerves and spinal cord work properly. The pupil reflex is also often tested with a small lamp.

Newborn babies have special **infant reflexes**. If you put a finger in their hand, they grasp it firmly, which is the grasp reflex. If you touch their cheek, they turn their head and search for the breast. These reflexes disappear again in the first months of life.

Besides inborn reflexes there are also learned ones, which are called **conditioned reflexes**. The Russian researcher Ivan Pavlov showed around 1900 that dogs produce saliva when they merely hear a tone that was previously always followed by food. In humans too, your mouth sometimes waters when you think of lemons. Such links are formed through experience.

begriffe.erklaerung: The path from the sensor through the spinal cord to the muscle.
Something that a sense organ perceives, for example heat or light.
A reflex that has come about through learning.

gewusst: Coughing, sneezing, swallowing and yawning are also reflexes.
A blink reflex lasts only about a tenth of a second.
Ivan Pavlov received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1904, but for his research on digestion.

teile.einleitung: Feeling nervous before an exam is completely normal. A little excitement can even help you to concentrate. But when the fear becomes so great that it blocks you, it is called exam anxiety, and there is a lot you can do about it.
wichtigste: In a blackout, you suddenly cannot think of anything because of fear.
Typical signs are a pounding heart, damp hands or tummy ache.
Negative self-talk such as “I won’t manage it anyway” strengthens the fear.
A study plan with fixed stages helps weeks before the exam.
A practice exam at home makes the situation more familiar.
Belly breathing calms you before and during the exam.
If the fear is strong, your teacher or the school psychology service can help.

abschnitte.text: Fear is really a protection programme of the body. It switches to alarm, as if it had to flee from a danger. Then the **heart** beats faster, the hands become damp, and the tummy tingles or hurts. Sometimes your head is suddenly empty, which is called a **blackout**. The knowledge is not gone, it is just blocked for a moment.

Thoughts such as “I won’t manage it anyway” or “Everyone else is better” are called **negative self-talk**. They make the fear bigger. It helps to replace them deliberately with kinder sentences, for example: “I have studied and I am doing my best.” A single exam does not decide your whole life either.

You can do something about exam anxiety **weeks ahead**. A **study plan with fixed stages** spreads the material over many small portions. That way you do not have to learn everything at once the evening before. A **practice exam at home** is very helpful: you solve old questions with a clock running. This makes the situation more **familiar**, and the brain has less reason for alarm. Enough sleep and exercise help as well.

A simple help is **belly breathing**: you breathe in slowly through your nose so that your tummy rises, and out even more slowly through your mouth. This calms the heart. If a blackout happens in the exam, you can **breathe deeply** and first solve an **easier question**. Often the knowledge then comes back by itself.

If the fear becomes very strong, you should not be left alone with it. In Switzerland you can turn to your **teacher** or to the **school psychology service**. Parents and friends can help too. The 147 helpline of Pro Juventute can also be reached around the clock.

gewusst: A moderate amount of excitement can even improve your performance in an exam.
If you explain the material to someone, you quickly notice what you already know well, and that builds self-confidence.

teile.einleitung: The pulse is the heartbeat that you can feel in blood vessels, for example at the wrist. It shows how often the heart beats per minute. Doctors and paramedics check the pulse to find out how a person is doing.
wichtigste: The pulse shows how often the heart beats per minute.
You can feel it at the wrist or at the neck.
In adults, the resting pulse is usually between 60 and 100 beats per minute.
Children have a faster pulse than adults.
With sport, excitement or fever, the pulse rises.
Trained athletes often have an especially low resting pulse.

abschnitte.text: With every heartbeat, the heart pumps a surge of blood into the arteries. This makes the vessel walls stretch briefly, like a wave in a garden hose. This **pulse wave** can be felt with the fingers in some places. The number of beats per minute is called the **pulse rate**.

Lay your index and middle finger on the inside of your wrist, below the thumb. That is where the **radial artery** lies. Count the beats for 15 seconds and multiply the result by four. You can also feel the pulse well at the neck, next to the larynx.

In adults at rest, the heart usually beats 60 to 100 times a minute. Children have a faster pulse, and in newborn babies it is over 100 beats. Well-trained endurance athletes often have a **resting pulse** of under 60, because their heart pumps more blood with every beat. The regularity of the pulse is also important.

When running or cycling, the muscles need more oxygen, so the pulse rises. Excitement, fear, heat, fever or coffee also make the heart beat faster. In sleep, on the other hand, the pulse falls. A pulse that is too fast is called **tachycardia**, one that is too slow bradycardia.

In an emergency, paramedics and doctors quickly check breathing and circulation. Today many people also measure their pulse with a sports watch or a fitness band. They use light to measure how the amount of blood under the skin changes. A very irregular pulse can be a sign of a heart disease.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of heartbeats per minute.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
The pulse when you are sitting or lying quietly.
A heartbeat that is too fast.

gewusst: In a long human life the heart beats about 2 to 3 billion times.
A shrew has a pulse of several hundred beats per minute, a blue whale only a few.
Even in ancient China, doctors examined the pulse very closely to recognise illnesses.

teile.einleitung: Not every stimulus is noticed. A sound can be too quiet, a light too weak. The **stimulus threshold** is the limit from which our senses only just perceive a stimulus.
wichtigste: The stimulus threshold is the smallest strength of stimulus that is only just perceived.
A stimulus below this threshold is called **subliminal**.
With age, the hearing threshold for high notes rises.
In the dark, the stimulus threshold of the eye falls, so you see weaker light.
The difference threshold is the smallest difference between two stimuli that you still notice.
A nerve cell sends its signal according to the all-or-nothing principle.

abschnitte.text: Every sense has a **stimulus threshold**. It is the smallest strength of a stimulus that you only just notice, for example the quietest audible sound. If a stimulus is weaker, it is called **subliminal**. It is there but is not consciously perceived. The threshold is not the same in everyone and can also change.

Sometimes it is not a question of whether you notice something, but whether you notice a difference. The **difference threshold** is the smallest difference between two stimuli that you can still tell apart. According to **Weber’s law**, it depends on the basic strength: if with 100 grams you only just notice 2 grams more, then with 1000 grams you need about 20 grams. So the difference must always make up roughly the same proportion. The law is named after the German researcher Ernst Heinrich Weber.

If you stay in the dark for a longer time, the stimulus threshold of the eye **falls**. You then see even very weak light, which is called dark adaptation. With increasing age, on the other hand, the hearing threshold for high notes **rises**, so they are heard less well. Pain also has a threshold. With sunburn the skin is inflamed, the pain threshold has fallen, and even a light touch hurts.

Individual **nerve cells** also have a threshold. If a stimulus stays below it, nothing happens. If the threshold is exceeded, the cell sends out a signal, and always at full strength. This principle is called the **all-or-nothing principle**. The brain recognises a strong stimulus by the cell sending more signals per second, not by stronger signals.

gewusst: Young people often hear high whistling tones that adults can no longer perceive at all.
It takes about half an hour until the eyes have got used to the darkness completely.

teile.einleitung: In **restless legs syndrome**, people feel a strong urge to move their legs in the evening and at rest. The condition can disturb sleep badly but is well treatable.
wichtigste: Another name is **Willis-Ekbom disease**.
The complaints occur at rest and in the evening and improve with movement.
Iron deficiency can trigger or strengthen the disease.
Dopamine agonists are often used.
In kidney failure the disease occurs especially often.
The diagnosis is made mainly from the complaints in conversation.

abschnitte.text: **Restless legs syndrome**, RLS for short, is a disease of the nervous system. It is also called **Willis-Ekbom disease**, after two doctors who described it. Those affected feel an unpleasant tingling, pulling or tightness in the legs. With this comes a strong urge to move the legs. The complaints occur **at rest** and above all **in the evening** or at night and **improve with movement**.

Because the complaints begin when lying down, many of those affected find it hard to fall asleep. In a sleep laboratory, sleep is studied with **polysomnography**, a measurement of many body values during the night. In many people with RLS it shows **periodic limb movements**, that is, regular twitches of the legs during sleep. During the day those affected are then often tired. That is why good treatment is important.

In many people no cause is known, and the disease often runs in families. Sometimes, though, another illness is behind it, and then it is called **secondary** RLS. An important trigger is **iron deficiency**. RLS occurs especially often in **kidney failure**, that is, when the kidneys work badly. The doctor makes the diagnosis mainly **in conversation** from the typical complaints.

With iron deficiency, it helps to add iron. **Dopamine agonists** are often used, medicines that work like the messenger substance dopamine. With longer use, **augmentation** can occur. This is a worsening of the complaints caused by the medicines themselves, which then appear earlier in the day or more strongly. In this case the doctor adjusts the treatment.

gewusst: As early as the 17th century, the English doctor Thomas Willis described the typical complaints.
A short walk or stretching exercises in the evening can ease the complaints.

teile.einleitung: REM sleep is a special phase of sleep. In it the eyes move quickly back and forth, and we dream especially vividly. Several times a night, REM sleep and other sleep phases alternate.
wichtigste: REM stands for “rapid eye movement”.
In REM sleep we dream especially vividly and in pictures.
Most skeletal muscles are almost completely relaxed during it.
The brain is almost as active as when awake.
In adults, REM sleep makes up about 20 to 25 per cent of the night.
Newborn babies spend about half of their sleep in REM sleep.

abschnitte.text: The abbreviation **REM** stands for the English **“rapid eye movement”**. During this phase of sleep, the eyes move quickly back and forth under the closed lids. REM sleep was discovered and described in the **1950s** by the American researchers **Eugene Aserinsky** and **Nathaniel Kleitman**. They observed sleepers in the laboratory.

In REM sleep we **dream** especially **vividly and in pictures**. If you wake someone in this phase, they can often remember their dream well. At the same time most **skeletal muscles are almost completely relaxed**. That makes sense: it means we do not act out the movements from our dreams. Only the eye muscles and the breathing muscles go on working.

REM sleep is also called **“paradoxical sleep”**. Paradoxical means contradictory. Although you are sleeping deeply, the **brain is almost as active as when awake**. **Heartbeat and breathing** also become **more irregular** than in the calm phases of sleep. Researchers suspect that REM sleep is important for processing what we have experienced and for consolidating what we have learned.

A night consists of several **sleep cycles** of about an hour and a half. In each cycle, light sleep, deep sleep and REM sleep follow one another. At the start of the night, the REM phases are short, and **towards morning** they last **longest**. In adults, REM sleep makes up about **20 to 25 per cent** of the night. **Newborn babies** even spend about **half** of their sleep in REM sleep.

gewusst: Many animals, for example dogs and cats, also have REM sleep. Sometimes their paws twitch.
If you wake from a dream in the morning, you have often just woken from a REM phase.

teile.einleitung: Proteins are vital building blocks of all living things. The body needs them to build muscles, cells and many important substances such as enzymes and hormones. They consist of long chains of small building blocks, the amino acids.
wichtigste: In German, proteins are also called Eiweisse.
The body needs proteins to build muscles, cells and many important substances.
Proteins consist of chains of amino acids.
For humans, 20 different amino acids are important.
Some amino acids must be taken in with food.
Enzymes, antibodies and many hormones are proteins.
Meat, fish, eggs, milk, pulses and nuts contain a lot of protein.

abschnitte.text: **Proteins** are large molecules made of many small building blocks, the **amino acids**. These line up one after another like beads on a string. Then the chain folds into a very particular shape. What job the protein does depends on this shape.

Muscles, skin, hair and nails consist to a large extent of proteins. **Enzymes** are proteins that speed up chemical reactions, for example in digestion. The red blood pigment haemoglobin transports oxygen, and antibodies fight off disease-causing agents. The hormone insulin is also a protein.

A lot of protein is found in meat, fish, eggs, milk, cheese and yoghurt. Plant foods such as lentils, beans, chickpeas, tofu and nuts are also good sources. In the gut, the proteins are broken down into amino acids. From these the body then builds its own proteins.

Adults need about 0.8 grams of protein per day for every kilogram of body weight. Children and teenagers who are growing need proportionally a little more. The body cannot make nine amino acids itself; they are called **essential amino acids**. A varied diet normally supplies enough of them.

The blueprint for every protein is stored in the **DNA**. In the cells, small factories called ribosomes read this plan. They join the amino acids together in the right order. In this way a human being can make tens of thousands of different proteins.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small building block from which proteins are put together.
A protein that speeds up chemical processes in the body.
An amino acid that you have to take in with food.
A tiny cell factory that builds proteins.

gewusst: When you fry an egg, the egg white turns white because the proteins change through the heat.
Spider silk is a protein and, in proportion to its weight, very strong.
The word protein comes from the Greek proteuo, meaning “I take first place”.
